Philips stock faces EUR 288 million Respironics settlement
sum: Philips is moving toward a settlement of long-running US investigations linked to its recalled Respironics sleep and respiratory devices. The company disclosed the agreement in principle with the US Department of Justice on Tuesday, November 3, while MedTech Dive reported the proposed resolution on November 4.

The agreement covers criminal and civil investigations related to the recall. Philips recorded a EUR 288 million provision for the proposed settlement, with payment expected in the first quarter of 2027. The agreement still requires final documentation, so the disclosure does not represent a completed payment or a fully executed settlement.

MedTech Dive reported that the recall involved more than 15 million devices, including continuous positive airway pressure and bilevel positive airway pressure machines as well as ventilators. The issue concerned soundproofing foam that could break down into particles and be inhaled by users.

The proposed payment would address the US Department of Justice investigations, but it does not remove every Respironics-related risk. MedTech Dive reported that the settlement is separate from a 2024 US Food and Drug Administration consent decree that restricts the sale of certain respiratory devices until Philips meets the agency's requirements.

Chief Executive Roy Jakobs said Philips was working toward a return to the US market for affected products, but that the timing ultimately depended on the FDA. The company is therefore continuing to prepare for a possible market return without controlling the authorization timetable.

The proposed settlement also excludes other proceedings, including an investigation by US state attorneys general. For investors, that distinction matters: the agreement can reduce one part of the legal overhang, but it does not establish that all recall-related liabilities have been resolved.

Philips stock traded at 27.37 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 11:08 CET on Friday, November 13, 0.44 percent above the Xetra close of Thursday, November 12. The comparison places the shares modestly higher during the session, without establishing that the move was caused by the settlement news.

Makeup artist draws on heritage for new palette
sum: Cover of Soualigan Divine Palette. The palette has been created in the shape of St. Maarten and weighs about 500 grams.

PHILIPSBURG--St. Peters-born makeup artist and entrepreneur Antoinette Philips is celebrating her heritage ahead of St. Maarten Day with the launch of a new eyeshadow palette inspired by the island's communities, landscapes and cultural symbols.

The palette, named Soualigan Divine, will be available from November 11 through Philips' beauty brand, VMOUR Beauty. Its 22 shades take their names from places and features associated with the island, including Grand Case, Dutch Quarter, the Salt Pond, Guavaberry and the flamboyant tree. One shade is named after St. Peters where Philips once resided.

Currently based in the Netherlands, where she works as a social worker supporting persons with disabilities, Philips developed the collection as a tribute to the island that shaped her identity. Both the palette's case design and its colours draw inspiration from St. Maarten and St. Martin as a shared island with two distinct national identities.

Soualigan Divine is the second palette released under VMOUR Beauty, which Philips established in 2024. Her first collection, VMOUR Merlot, reflected her interest in wine and makeup with packaging shaped like a wine glass.

The idea for the brand developed from informal makeup sessions with friends, often accompanied by a glass of wine. Encouraged by a mentor to share those moments online, Philips began livestreaming her makeup sessions and gradually built an audience on TikTok, where she shares makeup looks and interacts with followers.

With her latest collection, she has shifted the inspiration from wine to the Caribbean, drawing on the colours and cultural influences of her homeland. The palette combines matte and shimmer finishes, with shades intended for both everyday makeup and more dramatic looks.

items.t: Philips: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors
sum: On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 3, 2026, Philips (PHG -0.52%) announced an 8% increase in equipment order intake. For long-term investors, expanding order books signal that health systems are locking into the company's diagnostic platforms for years to come. Three things management said stand out.
1. Health Systems Are Prioritizing Clinical Value Over Upfront Price

Hospitals are consolidating vendor relationships to streamline operations, giving Philips an advantage in pitching integrated equipment platforms. Management captured market share in North America by replacing long-standing rivals at major hospital networks.

North America was particularly strong as health systems consolidate, purchasing decisions remain primarily driven by clinical differentiation, productivity gains, and long-term strategic value rather than price alone.
2. Subscription Models Are Building Predictable Healthcare Revenue

The company is shifting hospital clients away from one-off equipment sales and toward Enterprise Monitoring as a Service (EMaaS), a model in which health systems pay recurring fees for software and hardware. That recurring model helps insulate cash flows from lumpier capital spending cycles.

Our Enterprise Monitoring as a Service business model also continued to scale with revenues nearly doubling year-on-year, demonstrating steady progress in building more recurring and predictable revenue.

Commentary: CVS unwinds its big mergers, ending a dream of healthcare dominance
sum: I’m old enough to remember the day when CVS, the big drugstore company, opted to get even bigger by acquiring the health insurer Aetna.

“Today marks the start of a new day in healthcare and a transformative moment for our company and our industry,” CVS Health President and Chief Executive Officer Larry J. Merlo boasted. The $70-billion deal would lead to “improved health outcomes and lower medical costs,” he said.
I’m not giving away my age with this recollection. The deal happened a mere eight years ago, in 2018.
Merlo’s ambitions and braggadocio didn’t have much of a shelf life: On Wednesday, the company announced it was deconstructing the edifice he had erected, by splitting into two companies.
Greater independence will make it easier to serve consumers, members, patients, and communities.
— CVS Health CEO David Joyner, explaining the virtues of spinning off the company’s drugstores

One, encompassing Aetna and Caremark, the pharmacy benefit manager it acquired in 2007 for $26.5 billion, will retain the name CVS Health, and the other, dubbed CVS Pharmacy, will own the 9,000 CVS drugstores, the nationwide legacy of the original company that started with a single Massachusetts store.

Philips Q3 adjusted earnings rise as order intake strengthens
sum: Investing.com-- Koninklijke Philips (AS:PHG) shares climbed to an eight-month high on Tuesday after the Dutch health technology company reported stronger third-quarter adjusted earnings, supported by improved margins and robust order growth.
Shares rose 3.22% to €25.31, touching their highest level since March 5 and sharply outperforming the broader AEX index, which fell 0.2%.

Philips reported third-quarter comparable sales growth of 3% to €4.39 billion, around 40 basis points below company-compiled analyst consensus. Adjusted EBITA, however, increased 7.2% year on year to €569 million, beating consensus by around 9%. The adjusted EBITA margin expanded 70 basis points to 13%.

Comparable order intake increased 8%, driven by strong demand in Diagnosis & Treatment, where orders grew at a rate approaching 20%, with double-digit growth in both Image Guided Therapy and Precision Diagnosis, Citi said.

However, sales in the division were flat, as growth in Image Guided Therapy was offset by weaker Precision Diagnosis revenue. Connected Care recorded 5% comparable sales growth, while Personal Health increased 8%.

Citi described the quarter as mixed, noting that adjusted EBITA performance and Connected Care were stronger than expected. Although, it warned that sluggish Diagnosis & Treatment sales momentum raised questions about Philips' ability to achieve its 2027 and medium-term growth ambitions.
The bank also noted that Philips' 8% group order growth compared with 4% at GE HealthCare in the quarter, although its four-year cumulative order growth of 1.5% remained below GE HealthCare's 3%.

Trump Accounts: What parents need to know about automatic enrollment, $1,000 seed money and activation
sum: Whether you realize it or not, your child may be enrolled in a “Trump Account.”

Rolled out earlier this year, the Trump Accounts program allows parents to claim special investment accounts for children who are 18 years old or younger. And some babies are eligible to receive a one-time $1,000 contribution from the government.

Now, because of automatic enrollment highlighted Wednesday by President Trump, the Treasury Department says every eligible child with a valid Social Security number has a Trump Account. But parents and legal guardians would still need to formally activate the accounts if they haven’t already.

The accounts are a savings tool that invests money in the stock market on a child’s behalf. The child can’t access the money until they turn 18 and can use it only for specific purposes, such as paying tuition, starting a business or making a down payment on a home. Families can activate an account through the program’s trumpaccounts.gov website or its mobile phone app.

The government will make a $1,000 contribution for some babies after the account is claimed. To qualify for the $1,000 seed money, a baby must be a U.S. citizen, have a Social Security number and be born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028 — covering Trump’s current term.

Any parent — regardless of their immigration status — can open an account for a qualifying child. Parents of older children also are encouraged to open accounts. Even though they aren’t eligible for the government’s $1,000 contribution, some older children are eligible for seed money of $250 drawn from separate investments from wealthy donors.

Otherwise, family contributions will need to come out of pocket. Parents can contribute up to $2,500 annually in pretax income, much like retirement accounts. Employers, relatives, friends, local governments and philanthropic groups can also pitch in. Yearly contributions are capped at $5,000, although contributions from governments and charities don’t count toward that total.

items.t: Philips looks to make India its centre of excellence for innovation
sum: Dutch major Philips is doubling down on investments in research and development activities, and aims to make India a centre of excellence for innovation across its product segments.
By the end of this decade, Philips will be completing 100 years in India, which is also a strong growth driver for its personal healthcare portfolio.

At the global level, Philips spends about 5-6 per cent of its revenue in R&D against an average 2-3 per cent in the consumer industry globally, according to Deeptha Khanna, Executive Vice President and Chief Business Leader for personal health and a member of the Royal Philips executive committee in India.

She told PTI that it was quite bullish about India's role not just in terms of the market and growth opportunity but also being a centre of excellence for the company on innovation across the entire enterprise.
"I think that (5-6 per cent) is a really substantial commitment. So, we are pretty serious about first and foremost R&D investment.

"Also, 40 per cent of our personal care portfolio in India is local for locals. So, we do expect to make sure that our investment in both R&D and marketing and distribution, among others, will support our growth ambition," she said.

Without disclosing R&D investment numbers, Khanna said, "I think the investment is the people. The majority of our digital innovation teams are sitting here already right now, and I think that promises a lot of impact in the future".

items.t: Why Exor's shares still look deeply undervalued
sum: As the owner of Ferrari, Exor controls one of the world's highest-quality luxury assets, yet its shares reflect little of that strength. The investment case rests on three components: asset quality, capital allocation, and the discount to net asset value (NAV).

Ferrari is a high-margin luxury business with gross margins of about 50%. Growth is driven by deliberate supply discipline. Production is constrained to preserve exclusivity, resulting in sustained excess demand and multi-year order backlogs. This underpins both pricing power and earnings visibility.
Returns are driven by changes in underlying asset values, capital allocation decisions, movements in the discount to NAV.
The first two have been delivered historically, although future outcomes remain uncertain.

At about 50%, the current discount is wide in both absolute and historical terms. The opportunity lies in mean reversion. A narrowing towards the historical range implies material upside, even without underlying NAV growth.
The investment case does not rely on strong macro conditions. Instead, returns are driven by portfolio execution and the potential for discount normalisation.
On balance, the odds and probabilities favour a narrowing of the discount.

Forecasts indicate that the market will reach $20.33 billion in 2030, mirroring a CAGR of 21.3%. This growth will be fueled by increased telehealth investments, a heightened focus on preventive healthcare, the proliferation of AI-enabled health analytics, the rise of personalized healthcare solutions, and the integration of digital health with clinical workflows. Contributing trends include the growing adoption of remote patient monitoring devices and wearable health technologies, alongside the integration of cloud-based health platforms and continuous health data tracking.

The burgeoning demand for remote monitoring devices is a significant growth driver. These devices allow healthcare professionals to efficiently gather and evaluate patient data. For instance, the UK Parliament expanded digital systems to monitor vital signs for 500,000 more individuals in care settings as of March 2023. This increasing demand underscores the growth trajectory of the digital health monitoring devices market.

Technological innovation remains pivotal in this sector. In June 2024, Prevounce Health unveiled the Pylo GL1-LTE, a remote blood glucose monitoring device that integrates seamlessly with the Prevounce remote care management platform and ensures reliable data transmission across diverse cellular networks in the U.S. This innovation supports the expanding landscape of remote patient monitoring (RPM) programs for diabetes management.
In a significant industry move, Becton, Dickinson and Company acquired the Critical Care product group from Edwards Lifesciences in September 2024.

sum: Arterial IVUS Tutor is your fast-track to confident peripheral vascular IVUS imaging interpretation. An interactive program designed for health care professionals who want to improve their IVUS eyes. The image interpretation for PAD, AV access and AAA procedures is catered to all levels—beginner, intermediate, and advanced learners.

Based on nearly 20 hours of physician insights gathered globally, the Arterial IVUS Tutor app has been specifically developed to fulfill a significant need in vascular medicine: providing accessible and effective training for interpreting intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) images. This follows the established Venous IVUS Tutor, developed with the American Venous Forum (AVF), which is widely utilized international.

Although IVUS offers significant advancements for arterial procedures, interpreting its images presents notable challenges, and comprehensive educational resources are limited. Leading medical societies—including Society for Cardiovascular Angiography & Interventions (SCAI), AVF, American Vein & Lymphatic Society (AVLS), Society for Vascular Medicine (SVM), and Society for Vascular Surgery (SVS)—have emphasized the importance of developing enhanced educational tools to encourage broader IVUS adoption and address difficulties in image interpretation¹. Recent studies confirm these existing gaps, underscoring the pressing need for innovative solutions that support clinicians throughout their IVUS learning and practice.
I believe this app will be a powerful educational resource with real-world cases and detailed imaging, it can really help physicians deepen their understanding and improve patient care.

Philips shares surge 12% amid 'clear step up in sales'; European stocks close down
sum: European stocks finished Tuesday in negative territory amid a flurry of corporate earnings releases.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 ended the session down just below the flatline, reversing earlier gains, with most major bourses and sectors mixed.
Tuesday was a busy day for corporate earnings releases, with some of Europe's most prominent firms updating investors on their finances.
Among them is Philips, which published its full-year 2025 earnings before the bell on Tuesday morning.

The company posted comparable order intake growth of 6% and returned to profit following a net loss in 2024. It issued fresh guidance for 2026, saying it now expects comparable sales growth to fall in the range of 3% to 4.5%.

Net income for the year rose by 1.6 million euros ($1.9 million), which Philips attributed to higher income from operations, lower income tax charges, and smaller expenses. Separately, the company said Tuesday that it was proposing the reappointment of CEO Roy Jakobs, with the proposal to be submitted for shareholder approval at the firm's Annual General Meeting on May 8.

Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday, Jakobs said Philips' earnings contained "a lot of very good news," touting the 7% order intake growth, and growth in margins despite tariff headwinds.

Philips says it hasn’t released guidance after concerns sink stock
sum: Investing.com -- Philips stock fell 4% Thursday after the Dutch health technology company raised concerns about tariff headwinds and growth expectations during a Citi Global Healthcare Conference.

The decline marked the stock's steepest drop in nearly 10 months, with shares falling as much as 8.6% at one point, making it the worst performer on both the Stoxx 600 and the Stoxx 600 Health Care subindex.

According to Citi, Philips CEO Roy Jakobs cautioned that while organic sales growth would improve in 2026 from the approximately 2% expected this year, it was "unlikely" to double. This contrasts with current consensus estimates pointing to growth of 4.5%.
The company also warned that tariff headwinds next year are expected to almost double, potentially impacting profit margins despite Philips reiterating its goal to improve margins in 2026.

Regarding regional outlook, Philips indicated that the global hospital capital spending environment in 2026 would remain similar to 2025, with strong U.S. demand, solid European and international markets, but muted conditions in China.
Citi analyst Veronika Dubajova noted that Philips believes "a lack of growth opportunities in China is leading many of the Chinese manufacturers to pursue growth outside of China."

In response to the market reaction, Philips issued a statement reaffirming that its official 2026 outlook will be released as planned on February 10. The company emphasized it expects "comparative sales growth to accelerate sequentially in 2026 towards mid-single-digit growth" supported by "continued solid order momentum."
